notes.title: Chapter map: Agent runtime

headings.text: 🌳 Decide: where should this code run?

notes.html:
Where the agent actually runs: a server that takes jobs, one process per call, a session that runs the loop, your brain behind one node, and an API that stays out of the call. This section is the deployment half of the pillar; 09 Production covers scale and operations.

Where this sits

capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe

Reading order

# Note Tier Stage You'll understand
1 Agent server, jobs, isolation CORE carry registration, dispatch, warm processes, drain
2 Agent session and pipeline CORE think session vs agent, nodes, hooks, events
3 Handoffs, tasks, workflows SUPPORTING think LiveKit workflows vs owning the graph
4 Event-loop discipline SUPPORTING think why one blocking call is dead air
5 Control plane vs agent runtime SUPPORTING carry the four tiers and their scaling axes
– LiveKit Cloud vs self-hosted BREADTH carry managed vs your own servers

Owners

Concept Home
Dispatch, job lifecycle, prewarm, server options agent server
AgentSession, nodes, hooks, events agent session
Agents, tasks, task groups, supervisor and sub-agent hierarchies, handoffs; where decisions live; the four production workflows (consent, escalation, handoff, context) workflows
Loop lag, blocking calls, deadlines event loop
API vs runtime, four tiers control plane
Rooms, tracks, tokens (the media model) rooms, tracks, tokens and dispatch
Node counts and the vendor ceiling at scale scaling to 1,000 calls

Decide: where should this code run?

Ask in order If yes → Because
1. Does it run for the length of a call, in real time? agent process (a job) isolation, warm models, one loop per call
2. Is it a short request (token, room, record)? control plane stateless, scales on requests
3. Can it run after the call and be retried? queue + after-call worker survives process death, scales to zero
4. Is it CPU-heavy inside a call? a process pool, never the loop the loop is soft real-time

🔊 Our system in one table

What Value Status
Agent server AgentServer(setup_fnc=prewarm, shutdown_process_timeout=120), explicit dispatch meghdootam
Session Silero, Deepgram, LangGraph via LLMAdapter, FallbackAdapter TTS, audio turn detector
Brain own LangGraph; no LiveKit handoffs
Control plane FastAPI: 30-min room-scoped token with dispatch metadata
Hosting LiveKit Cloud (design: self-hosted, in region) /
Loop-lag metric designed, not built
After-call scoring in the shutdown hook today; queue + worker designed /

Game Day

Q27 why LiveKit · Q29 token, room, dispatch · Q30 FastAPI is not the runtime · Q48 isolation and the event loop

notes.title: Agent Server, Jobs and Process Isolation
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Job lifecycle, Server options, Agent dispatch (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/media_transport/livekit_decision.md Per-session process isolation · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/main.py, dispatch.py

TL;DR

An agent server (worker) registers with LiveKit and waits. When a room needs an agent, LiveKit dispatches a job; the server runs it in its own process, prewarmed with models already loaded. One process per call means one call's crash or blocking code can't hurt another, and scaling is "more processes".

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per session

Flow: server registersperson joins with a token that names the agentLiveKit dispatches a joba warm process takes itentrypoint joins the roomsession runsshutdown hooksprocess ends

Recall

Prompt Answer
What a job is one agent's work in one room, run in its own process
Automatic vs explicit dispatch every room vs only when asked by name (recommended)
Two ways to dispatch explicitly in the participant's token (RoomAgentDispatch), or the API (CreateDispatch)
Where dispatch data goes ctx.job.metadata, up to 512 KiB
What prewarm does loads models in idle processes before any job arrives
Draw one server with three processes, one crashing the crash ends only its own call

The idea

Without it: many calls share one event loop and one memory space; one blocking call or memory leak becomes dead air for every caller on that machine.

It does: gives each call a process, a warm start, a clean shutdown, and a load signal so LiveKit sends new jobs to servers with room.

It costs: memory per process (each loads its models), and a process start that must be hidden by keeping idle processes warm.

How it works

Option (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Default Does
num_idle_processes Python ceil(cpu_count) (0 in dev) warm processes waiting for jobs
load_fnc / load_threshold 5 s average CPU / 0.7 above the threshold the server stops taking jobs
drain_timeout 1 hour on shutdown, live calls may finish
shutdown_process_timeout 10 s time for shutdown hooks before the process is killed
health port 8081 in production for the orchestrator's probes

Knobs

Knob Raise it → Lower it →
Idle processes no cold start under a burst; more idle memory cold starts on bursts
Load threshold denser servers, more risk of CPU-starved calls more servers, safer turns
Drain timeout long calls finish on deploy faster rollouts, cut calls
Shutdown timeout room for after-call work faster cleanup

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Server AgentServer(setup_fnc=prewarm, shutdown_process_timeout=120) main.py: the after-call Panel runs in the shutdown hook, 10–30 s
Prewarm Silero VAD loaded per idle process prewarm()
Dispatch explicit, in the candidate's token; metadata carries candidate, plan, resume point dispatch.py: the agent never arrives before the candidate
One process per interview yes LiveKit job model
Target after-call scoring moves to a queue and a separate worker ADD §2.3, N7

Measure it

  • Metric — job start time (dispatch → agent in room), jobs rejected for load, process crashes, memory per process.
  • See it — server logs and the health endpoint; ctx.log_context_fields puts the room on every log line.
  • Bounded by — load threshold, drain on deploy, and per-process isolation.

Pitfalls

Doing after-call work in the shutdown hook

  • Why it's tempting: the transcript is right there in memory.
  • Why it's wrong: if the process is killed, the work and the report are lost; and the hook's timeout caps how long it may run.
  • Think instead: enqueue the job durably and score in a separate worker.

Automatic dispatch in production

  • Why it's tempting: zero configuration.
  • Why it's wrong: the agent joins every room, with no metadata about who or what the call is.
  • Think instead: explicit dispatch by name, with metadata in the token.

Connections

capture → carry → … — where the agent's process comes from.

  • hosts the agent session.
  • isolates each call's event loop.
  • scaled in scaling to 1,000 calls.
  • Say it: Q29 · Q48

notes.title: The Agent Session and Its Pipeline — Session, Agent, Nodes, Hooks
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Agent sessions, Pipeline nodes & hooks (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/main.py (AgentSession)

TL;DR

The session runs the loop (listen, transcribe, decide the turn, call the brain, speak, handle interruptions) and owns the models; the agent holds instructions and tools. Every stage is a node you can override, and hooks let you act at turn boundaries. Override a node to change one stage; never fork the loop.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per session

Flow: AgentSession(vad, stt, llm, tts, turn_handling)listeningthinkingspeaking…drain speechclose

Recall

Prompt Answer
Session vs agent the loop and models vs instructions and tools
The session's states listening, thinking, speaking (plus user states)
Node to change text before speech tts_node (or tts_text_transforms)
Node to plug in your own brain llm_node, or an LLM adapter
Hook after the user's turn, before the reply on_user_turn_completed
Draw the session with its four model slots and three nodes you'd override vad/stt/llm/tts in; stt_node, llm_node, tts_node

The idea

Without it: you write the loop yourself: audio buffering, VAD, endpointing, streaming, interruption, transcripts, metrics. That's most of a voice agent's bugs.

It does: gives you the loop, with seams at every stage so your logic replaces one piece, not the whole.

It costs: a framework version to pin (hook names move between releases) and defaults you must read, because they decide behaviour (preemptive_generation is on by default).

How it works

Node or hook Override to Our use
stt_node preprocess audio, post-process text –
llm_node change chat context, tool calls, custom provider the LangGraph brain via an adapter (LLMAdapter(graph, stream_mode="custom"))
tts_node chunking, pronunciation, custom engine sentence chunking, lexicon, one stream per segment
transcription_node clean text sent to the client –
on_enter / on_exit greet, hand off, clean up –
on_user_turn_completed inject context, edit or abort the turn, quick filler echo guard drops turns here (StopResponse)

Session options worth knowing (Oct 2026): turn_handling (detector, endpointing, interruption, preemptive generation) · max_tool_steps 3 · user_away_timeout 15 s · tts_text_transforms · RoomOptions (noise cancellation on input, close_on_disconnect, delete_room_on_close). Events: agent_state_changed, user_state_changed, user_input_transcribed, conversation_item_added (carries per-turn metrics), close.

Knobs

Knob Default Trade
preemptive_generation on earlier replies vs wasted calls
max_tool_steps 3 longer tool chains vs runaway loops
user_away_timeout 15 s when the session marks the user away
Custom nodes none control vs upgrade friction

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Session Silero (prewarmed), Deepgram STT, LangGraph brain, FallbackAdapter TTS, turn_handling with the audio turn detector main.py
Brain seam LiveKit owns audio, VAD, turns, interruption, STT/TTS; LangGraph owns what to say next livekit_decision The LangGraph seam
Only one node writes speech respond, through get_stream_writer(); other nodes' tokens are never spoken hot_path.py
Framework pin livekit-agents 1.8.2 uv.lock

Measure it

  • Metric — per-turn metrics on conversation_item_added; state transitions per turn.
  • See it — log agent_state_changed and user_state_changed; our log shows user listening → speaking.
  • Bounded by — the framework's turn and interruption handling; your nodes stay small.

Pitfalls

Streaming every graph token to TTS

  • Why it's tempting: the default adapter mode speaks whatever the model emits.
  • Why it's wrong: internal nodes (classifiers, planners) get read aloud.
  • Think instead: let exactly one node write spoken text (stream_mode="custom").

Upgrading the framework without re-reading defaults

  • Why it's tempting: minor versions look safe.
  • Why it's wrong: defaults and hook names change (the text turn detector is being removed in 2.0; adaptive interruption became default on Cloud).
  • Think instead: pin the version, read the changelog, re-run the goldens.

Connections

… → think → … — the loop every stage note plugs into.

  • runs inside a job process.
  • hands decisions to your own graph or LiveKit workflows.
  • configured by turn handling and the TTS node.
  • Say it: Q27

notes.title: Handoffs, Tasks and Workflows — LiveKit's Tools vs Owning the Graph
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Workflows (read 16 Oct 2026) · Tasks & task groups, Supervisor, Subagent delegation, WarmTransferTask (read 17 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/media_transport/livekit_decision.md The LangGraph seam · Voice agents (agentic pillar)

TL;DR

LiveKit gives you agents (long-lived control, can hand off), tasks (short work that returns a typed result) and task groups (ordered steps that share context). Use them when the conversation is a sequence of roles or forms. When the conversation's decision logic is the product (scoring, coverage, budgets), own it in your own graph and let LiveKit run only the loop.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

Flow: is the logic a sequence of roles or forms?LiveKit agents + tasksown graph behind the LLM node

Recall

Prompt Answer
Agent vs task long-lived control vs a unit of work returning a typed result
What a handoff does fully transfers control; the old agent stops participating
Context on handoff explicit: pass chat_ctx, summarise, or start fresh
Task group ordered tasks sharing context; the person can go back; a summary returns to the parent
Sub-agent delegation a slower, stronger model works silently; the primary agent voices its result
Warm vs cold transfer to a human the human is briefed with history first vs just rings; caller holds, then calls merge
When to split into agents bloated instructions, conflicting tools, multi-turn collection, backtracking
Our split LiveKit: audio, turns, STT, TTS · LangGraph: what to say next
The four production workflows recording consent, escalate to humans, handoff between agents, preserve context
Draw both options for a three-phase interview handoffs between three agents vs one graph with phases

The idea

Without a choice: half the logic lives in LiveKit agents and half in a graph, and nobody knows which one decides the next question.

It does: puts each decision in one place: the framework for conversational plumbing, your graph for domain logic.

It costs: owning the graph means re-implementing what tasks give you (typed collection, backtracking); using tasks means your domain logic follows the framework's release cycle.

How it works

Need LiveKit workflows Own graph behind llm_node
Collect a name, email, date prebuilt tasks (GetEmailTask, …) hand-written
Hand off to a specialist agent handoff a phase in the graph
Scoring, coverage, per-question budgets awkward natural
Deterministic move selection (rules, not a model) possible natural
Tests without audio LiveKit unit tests plain graph tests
Survives framework upgrades follows LiveKit's API only the adapter changes

Multi-step workflows and hierarchies (LiveKit tasks, supervisor and sub-agent pages, read 17 Oct 2026)

Structure Who speaks to the person Control returns? Context Use when
One agent + tools the agent – one chat context default; 5–10 tools
Task (AgentTask[T]) the task, while it runs yes, with a typed result via complete() empty unless chat_ctx passed (copy(exclude_instructions=True)) one focused objective: consent, an email, a verification
Task group (TaskGroup, experimental) each task in turn yes: task_results by id, plus a summary merged into the parent (summarize_chat_ctx, default on) shared across the group's tasks ordered steps; the person can go back ("actually, change the date") and the model can regress to an earlier task by id
Supervisor + tasks the task while it runs, then the supervisor yes the supervisor passes a copy without its instructions one agent must keep the whole conversation in view while delegating focused work
Sub-agent delegation never the sub-agent: the primary voices its result, maybe turns later yes, asynchronously (ctx.update() makes the tool non-blocking) the sub-agent has its own context slow reasoning on a stronger model while a fast model keeps talking; omit ctx.update() if the answer must be verified first
Handoff the new agent no: the old agent stops explicit: chat_ctx, a summary, or fresh; pending async results are dropped unless in an AsyncToolset a different role with different instructions and tools

Rules for hierarchies in voice: one voice at a time (only the active agent or task speaks); await tasks only from on_enter, on_exit or a tool body; validate a task's result by value before acting on it; keep domain reasoning out of the supervisor's prompt; pass history only when the step needs it.

Our system, mapped: the interview's phases (greet → questions → wrap) play the part of a task group inside our own graph; T1 background analysis is sub-agent delegation (stronger model, silent, result used at the next turn); the voice is always the one respond node, so there is never a second speaker. No LiveKit tasks, supervisor or handoffs are used.

Production workflows (talk slide shared 16 Oct 2026): four flows every deployed voice agent needs, whichever side owns the logic.

Workflow When How (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Carry over Ours
Collect recording consent before any recording starts an opening task or line; record only after a yes; record: { redaction: true } per session the consent decision, on the session record recording off, because nobody was asked (recording and PII)
Escalate to humans the person asks; repeated failure (STT confidence, tool errors); high-stakes or abusive turns WarmTransferTask (phone), or a human joins the room as a participant; the agent says what happens next a short summary, the transcript, what was tried no live escalation: a practice tool; abuse ends the session; integrity flags go to a human after the call
Handoff between agents instructions bloat, tools conflict, a distinct role agent handoff; tasks and task groups explicit: chat_ctx, a summary, or a fresh start one graph, phases instead of agents
Preserve context across handoffs, reconnects, pauses, and long calls pass chat_ctx or a summary; keep state in the session, not the prompt facts and decisions, not every word a paused interview resumes from the next question (continue_from in the dispatch metadata); last 8 messages kept verbatim (RECENT_TURNS)

Rule: a handoff or escalation must never make the person repeat themselves; carry a summary, and say out loud what is happening.

Warm handoff to a human (LiveKit WarmTransferTask, read 17 Oct 2026)

Cold transfer Warm transfer
The human gets a ringing call the conversation history and context first
The caller repeats everything continues where they were
Cost none a second call leg, a briefing step
WarmTransferTask (Oct 2026) Detail
Dial sip_call_to (number or SIP URI) + sip_trunk_id (or LIVEKIT_SIP_OUTBOUND_TRUNK); sip_number caller ID; dtmf after answer
Caller side hold_audio (default BuiltinAudioClip.HOLD_MUSIC); caller I/O off during the transfer
Human side tools connect_to_caller, decline_transfer (with a reason), voicemail_detected; extra_instructions shape the briefing
No answer after ringing_timeout the task fails with ToolError and the caller conversation resumes: say so and offer another path
Result WarmTransferResult.human_agent_identity
Needs a SIP outbound trunk; Python beta.workflows, Node.js workflows

In a browser call (no phone network) the same pattern is a human joining the room as a participant after reading the summary. Our interviews have no live human handoff.

Knobs

Knob Trade
Where the decision lives framework convenience vs domain control
Context carried on handoff continuity vs prompt size

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Decision logic LangGraph: rules pick the move, respond phrases it, T1 in the background livekit_decision The LangGraph seam; hot_path.py
LiveKit handoffs and tasks not used –

Measure it

  • Metric — share of turns decided by rules vs a model; tests per decision path.
  • See it — CHAIR … → <move> (reason) log lines.
  • Bounded by — one owner per decision.

Pitfalls

Mixing handoffs with an external graph

  • Why it's tempting: each looks useful for a different part.
  • Why it's wrong: two systems now track who is in control; a handoff can bypass the graph's budgets.
  • Think instead: pick one owner for "what happens next".

Connections

… → think → … — where the brain plugs in.

  • plugs into the session's LLM node.
  • is the runtime half of latency-tiered agents.
  • design patterns in conversational and interview agents.
  • Say it: Q39

notes.title: Event-Loop Discipline — One Blocking Call Is Dead Air
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/utkarsh_architecture.md §2.4, §10 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/decision_rationale.md weak point 6 · Python — asyncio developing guide

TL;DR

The agent's turn-taking, streaming and background work share one async event loop per call. Any synchronous call on it (a blocking SDK, a big json.loads, a regex over a long transcript, a cold TLS handshake) stops everything, and the symptom isn't an error: it's silence on a live call. Keep CPU work off the loop, put deadlines on background tasks, and measure loop lag.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: background task blocks 300 msloop can't send audio or read VADperson hears a gapno exception anywhere

Recall

Prompt Answer
The symptom of a blocked loop dead air, not an error
Common culprits sync SDKs, tokenisers, large json.loads, regex over long text, cold TLS
Where CPU work goes a process pool, or the after-call worker
The metric event-loop lag, alert at 50 ms
What process-per-call changes the blast radius is one call, not every call on the pod
Draw a loop timeline with a 300 ms blocking call audio frames stop, VAD stops, then everything bursts

The idea

Without it: a harmless-looking library call in background analysis blocks the loop, and the agent stutters on calls that are otherwise healthy.

It does: treats the loop as soft real-time: nothing on it may take more than a few milliseconds of CPU.

It costs: discipline in every code review, and a lag metric nobody can skip.

How it works

Rule Because
Every background task has a deadline and is cancellable a hung task must not pile up across turns
CPU work leaves the loop (ProcessPoolExecutor) or the call the GIL and the loop serialise it otherwise
Warm connection pools at session start no TLS handshake mid-call
Measure loop lag directly it replaces the isolation a service split would have given
Escape hatch: two loops in one process T0 on its own thread, only if the metric demands it

Knobs

Knob Design value Trade
Lag alert p99 > 50 ms sensitivity vs noise
Background deadlines 0.9–1.8 s per agent richer analysis vs pile-up

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Process per interview yes, so a blocked loop affects one call LiveKit job model
Loop-lag metric and alert utkarsh_event_loop_lag_ms, alert at 50 ms ADD §10; not built
Weak point conceded "a rule, not a guarantee: one sync SDK call is dead air" decision_rationale weak point 6

Measure it

  • Metric — loop lag p99 per call (schedule a timer, measure how late it fires).
  • See it — Python asyncio debug mode logs callbacks over 100 ms (loop.slow_callback_duration).
  • Bounded by — deadlines on background tasks; per-call processes.

Pitfalls

Trusting async def to mean non-blocking

  • Why it's tempting: the function is async, so it must yield.
  • Why it's wrong: a sync call inside it blocks the loop all the same.
  • Think instead: check what each library does underneath; run CPU work in a pool.

Connections

… → think → … — the hidden cause of silence.

  • contained by process isolation.
  • threatens every background tier task.
  • Say it: Q48

notes.title: Control Plane vs Agent Runtime — Why the API Server Doesn't Run the Call
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/runtime_topology.md Decision 2 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/scaling_1k.md §1, §2.1

TL;DR

The control plane (an API like FastAPI) mints tokens, creates rooms, records sessions and handles webhooks: short, stateless requests. The agent runtime runs a 45-minute conversation in its own process. Mixing them puts long-lived, real-time work on a server built for short requests, and couples two different scaling axes.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per session

Flow: browsercontrol plane: token + dispatchbrowser joins roomLiveKit dispatchesagent runtime runs the call

Recall

Prompt Answer
Control plane does tokens, rooms, session records, webhooks
Agent runtime does the call itself, one process each
Why not run calls in API worker threads? one blocking STT or model call starves the shared loop; no per-call isolation
Webhook rule idempotent and fast: return 200, enqueue heavy work
Replicas for 1,000 calls (plan) 3–6 API replicas, off the media path
Draw the four tiers control plane · media (SFU) · agents · after-call workers

The idea

Without it: an API process holds calls for 45 minutes, can't be restarted without dropping them, and scales on the wrong signal.

It does: keeps the API stateless and cheap, and lets the agent tier scale on concurrent calls.

It costs: two deployables and a contract between them (the token API and the dispatch metadata).

How it works

Tier Runs Scales on Nodes
Control plane token mint, rooms, lifecycle, webhooks CPU / requests on-demand, small
Media (SFU) WebRTC routing, TURN tracks, nodes on-demand only (live media)
Agents one process per call concurrent calls on-demand
After-call workers scoring queue depth, to zero spot

Knobs

Knob Trade
Token lifetime shorter: safer if leaked, more refresh paths
What the token carries explicit dispatch + metadata vs a lookup at join

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Control plane FastAPI ("Aditya"): token, room, webhooks runtime_topology Decision 2
Token 30-minute, room-scoped JWT with explicit agent dispatch as_built row 2
Agent runtime LiveKit Agents worker, one process per interview main.py
Four-tier split at scale as above scaling_1k §1

Measure it

  • Metric — token-to-join time, webhook latency and retries, API p95.
  • See it — API logs keyed by room; LiveKit webhook delivery logs.
  • Bounded by — idempotent webhooks; the API never holds call state.

Pitfalls

Keeping call state in the API "for convenience"

  • Why it's tempting: the API already knows the session.
  • Why it's wrong: it can no longer scale freely or restart without breaking calls.
  • Think instead: state lives in the agent process and the database; the API only reads and writes records.

Connections

capture → carry → … — the request path before the call starts.

  • dispatches agent jobs.
  • scaled in scaling to 1,000 calls.
  • Say it: Q30 · Q45

notes.title: LiveKit Cloud vs Self-Hosted
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/media_transport/livekit_decision.md Options considered · LiveKit — Deploy agents (read 16 Oct 2026)

TL;DR

LiveKit is open source (Apache 2.0), so the same SFU and agent framework can run managed (LiveKit Cloud) or on your own servers. Cloud is fastest to start; self-hosting buys region control, data residency and cost at scale, and costs you a third system to operate.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

The idea

LiveKit Cloud Self-hosted
Start one CLI deploy; builds, secrets, logs, log drains, dashboard (Oct 2026) Kubernetes, nodes, TURN, Redis for multi-node
Extras Agent Insights, adaptive interruption, LiveKit Inference – (open-source parts only)
Region and residency their regions yours
Cost at scale usage-priced infrastructure + people
Rule – live media never on spot nodes (the coturn incident)

🔊 In our system

The ADR chose self-hosted (Cloud rejected on N3 and N7); the build runs on LiveKit Cloud (as_built "differs from the design" table). Target: self-hosted in the candidates' region, multi-node with Redis. /

Connections

sets where agent servers run; region choice in region placement.
